lead: A sample mean is not a fixed number; draw a new sample and it changes. Its sampling distribution describes that change, with centre μ and spread σ/√n. The sample variance has its own law, tied to chi-square for normal data. These two distributions turn a sample into an estimate with a known error. Engineers use them in quality control, A/B tests and average load checks, such as the mean time to settle a UPI payment. This chapter gives the formulas and the normal and chi-square results, without re-teaching the central limit theorem.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for random samples and statistics, Unit 3 for the normal distribution, and Unit 4 for the central limit theorem.

sections.h3: The sample mean and its standard error

blocks.text: Suppose X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ are n independent observations from a population with mean μ and variance σ². The sample mean is x̄ = (Σ Xᵢ)/n. It is a random variable: before you draw the sample, each Xᵢ is random, so x̄ is random. Its sampling distribution is the probability distribution of x̄ over repeated samples of size n.

For any random sample with finite σ², E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n. The standard error of x̄ is SE(x̄) = σ/√n. It measures the typical distance between x̄ and μ. Quadrupling n halves the standard error. When σ is unknown, replace it by the sample standard deviation s and call s/√n the estimated standard error. Write the word estimated in reports.

By the central limit theorem (see Unit 4), for large n, x̄ is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n), even when the population is not normal. If the population is normal, this result is exact for every n. The figure shows μ = 50, σ = 10 and n = 4, 16, 25; the curve narrows as n rises.

blocks.where: x̄ is the sample mean; Xᵢ is the ith observation; n is the sample size.

blocks.text: E(x̄) = μ, Var(x̄) = σ²/n, SE(x̄) = σ/√n
blocks.where: μ is the population mean; σ is the population standard deviation; SE is the standard error.

sections.h3: The sample variance and its chi-square distribution

blocks.text: The sample variance is S² = Σ(Xᵢ − x̄)²/(n−1). The n deviations Xᵢ − x̄ always add to zero, so only n−1 of them can vary freely. Dividing by n−1 instead of n makes E(S²) = σ² for a random sample. So S² is an unbiased estimator of the population variance (see Chapter 5.4).

If the population is normal, the exact sampling distribution is chi-square: (n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²ₙ₋₁. Here χ²ₙ₋₁ is the chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom (df). The df count is the number of independent pieces of information left after x̄ has been used to estimate μ. For a normal population, x̄ and S² are independent. That independence is special to normal samples and is used to build t and F statistics (see Chapter 5.3).
The mean of a χ²ᵥ variable is ν. Put ν = n−1: E[(n−1)S²/σ²] = n−1, so E(S²) = σ². Do not use the chi-square law for small samples from a non-normal population; it needs the normal population.

blocks.where: S² is the sample variance; Xᵢ is the ith observation; x̄ is the sample mean; n is the sample size.
n is the sample size; S² is the sample variance; σ² is the population variance; χ²ₙ₋₁ is chi-square with n−1 df; the result requires a normal population.

sections.h3: Using the standard error in practice

blocks.text: To standardise x̄, subtract μ and divide by the standard error: Z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n). When x̄ is normal, Z is standard normal, so you can read probabilities from the normal table (Unit 3). Use σ/√n when σ is known. When σ is unknown and the population is normal, use s/√n and the t distribution (see Chapter 5.3).

If you sample without replacement from a finite population of size N, the variance of x̄ is multiplied by the finite population correction (N−n)/(N−1). Then SE(x̄) = (σ/√n)√((N−n)/(N−1)). This is an extension. Most problems in this chapter assume an infinite population or sampling with replacement, so the correction is 1.
For a non-normal population and small n, the normal curve for x̄ may be poor. A common rough rule is n ≥ 30, but no single number is exact. If the population is very skewed, use a larger n.

blocks.where: Z is the standard normal variable; x̄ is the sample mean; μ is the population mean; σ is the population standard deviation; n is the sample size.
N is the population size; n is the sample size; the square-root factor is the finite population correction.

figure.caption: The three normal curves show the sampling distribution of x̄ for μ = 50, σ = 10 and n = 4, 16, 25. As n rises, the curve narrows and becomes taller; the standard error falls from 5 to 2.5 to 2.

spec.aria: Normal curves for the sample mean when sigma is 10 and sample sizes are 4, 16 and 25; the curve narrows as n rises.

examples.question: A normal population has mean μ = 50 and standard deviation σ = 10. A sample of n = 25 is drawn. Find P(46 ≤ x̄ ≤ 54).
steps: From the standard normal table, P(−2 ≤ Z ≤ 2) ≈ 0.954.
So the probability is about 0.954, or 95.4%.
examples.check:
import math
mu = 50
sigma = 10
n = 25
se = sigma / math.sqrt(n)
z1 = (46 - mu) / se
z2 = (54 - mu) / se
p = 0.5 * (math.erf(z2 / math.sqrt(2)) - math.erf(z1 / math.sqrt(2)))
print(round(se, 4))
print(round(z1, 4))
print(round(z2, 4))
print(round(p, 3))

traps: Using s/√n but calling it σ/√n. When σ is unknown, say estimated standard error.
Treating x̄ as normal for small n from a non-normal population. The central limit theorem needs large n; the normal result is exact only for a normal population.
Using denominator n in S² and then comparing to chi-square with n df. The correct df is n−1 because μ is estimated by x̄.
Applying (n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²ₙ₋₁ to non-normal data with small n. The exact chi-square law needs a normal population.
Confusing the population standard deviation σ with the standard error σ/√n. The standard error shrinks as n rises; σ does not.

quiz.q: Define the sampling distribution of x̄.
quiz.a: It is the probability distribution of x̄ over all repeated samples of size n from the population.

quiz.q: Why divide by n−1 in S²?
quiz.a: The n deviations from x̄ sum to zero, so only n−1 are free. Dividing by n−1 makes E(S²) = σ².

quiz.q: A normal population has μ = 100 and σ = 20. A sample of n = 16 is drawn. Find P(95 ≤ x̄ ≤ 105).
A normal sample of n = 10 gives S² = 16. If σ² = 25, compute (n−1)S²/σ² and its df.
Five hundred samples of n = 5 from a highly skewed population give a skewed histogram of x̄. Does this contradict the central limit theorem?
quiz.a: No. The central limit theorem is a large-n result. With n = 5 the normal approximation may be poor; exact normality of x̄ needs a normal population.

quiz.q: Why is the independence of x̄ and S² useful for normal samples?
quiz.a: For normal samples, t = (x̄ − μ)/(S/√n) = Z/√(χ²ₙ₋₁/(n−1)), where Z ~ N(0,1) and χ²ₙ₋₁ are independent. This quantity has n−1 df, and it gives the t tests and t intervals.

quiz.q: What is the standard error of x̄, and how is it estimated?
quiz.a: SE(x̄) = σ/√n. When σ is unknown, estimate it by s/√n.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the standard error of a mean is used in statistical process control, A/B testing and load testing; the chi-square law of S² feeds variance checks. Modern practice adds the bootstrap, which estimates the sampling distribution by resampling when formulas are hard. Regression software reports standard errors for coefficients using the same ideas. Search next: bootstrap standard error, Welch t-test, and sampling distribution of regression coefficients.
